stem: A training loss is very low, but validation loss has begun increasing for several epochs. What phenomenon is most directly indicated?

options.A: Overfitting: optimization on the training data is continuing while out-of-sample performance degrades.
options.B: Underfitting caused by insufficient model capacity.
options.C: A guarantee that the test distribution equals the training distribution.

rationales.correct: A widening train/validation gap with worsening validation loss is a classic signal that the model is fitting idiosyncrasies of the training set.
rationales.B: Underfitting typically produces poor training performance as well.
rationales.C: Validation behavior cannot establish distribution identity.
rationales.D: Loss curves do not guarantee calibrated probabilities.

stem: In penalized empirical risk minimization, what is the primary statistical role of regularization?

options.A: To constrain model complexity or parameter magnitude to trade some training fit for potentially better generalization.
options.C: To make the training set larger without collecting data.
options.D: To eliminate measurement noise from the labels.

rationales.correct: Regularization encodes a preference for simpler parameterizations or functions, often reducing variance at the cost of some training fit.
rationales.B: Regularization can increase training error by design.
rationales.C: It changes the objective, not the sample count.
rationales.D: It does not directly clean labels.

stem: For L1-regularized linear models, why can some coefficients become exactly zero?

options.A: The absolute-value penalty has a subgradient structure that creates sparse optima under suitable conditions.
options.B: L1 literally deletes random columns from the dataset before training.
options.C: L1 changes every feature into a binary feature.
options.D: L1 guarantees that all coefficients are nonzero.

rationales.correct: The kink of |w_j| at zero makes zero a favorable optimum for some coordinates when the data-fit gradient is not large enough to overcome the penalty.
rationales.B: Feature selection is an optimization consequence, not random column deletion.
rationales.C: The feature representation is not automatically binarized.
rationales.D: L1 is associated with sparsity, not dense solutions.

stem: In scikit-learn LogisticRegression, the parameter C controls regularization strength. What happens as C becomes smaller?

options.C: The optimizer necessarily switches from L2 to L1.
options.D: The number of classes is reduced.

rationales.correct: C is the inverse of regularization strength in scikit-learn's formulation: smaller C means stronger regularization.
rationales.C: The penalty choice is controlled separately.
rationales.D: C does not alter the class set.

stem: A model has high bias and high training error. Which intervention is most directly motivated by that diagnosis?

options.A: Increase effective model capacity, improve features, or reduce excessive regularization.
options.B: Add more regularization before changing anything else.
options.C: Use the test set to choose hyperparameters repeatedly.

rationales.correct: High bias means the current hypothesis class or training setup is systematically unable to fit the signal. More capacity, better representation, or less regularization are standard responses.
rationales.C: Repeated test-set tuning causes optimistic evaluation.
rationales.D: Permuting labels destroys the supervised signal.

stem: Why can increasing model capacity sometimes improve both training and validation performance before eventually hurting validation performance?

options.A: Additional capacity can first reduce underfitting, then cross into a regime where variance/overfitting dominates.
options.B: Validation error must monotonically increase with capacity.
options.C: Higher capacity always removes bias without affecting variance.
options.D: Capacity changes only inference latency, never statistical performance.

rationales.correct: The bias-variance tradeoff is not simply 'more complex is worse': early capacity gains can capture real structure, while excessive flexibility can fit noise.
rationales.B: The validation curve can be non-monotonic.
rationales.C: Capacity can affect both bias and variance.
rationales.D: Capacity directly affects fitting behavior and generalization.

stem: Dropout during neural-network training is best understood as which mechanism?

options.A: Randomly masking activations/units during training to discourage co-adaptation and act as a form of stochastic regularization.
options.B: Permanently deleting neurons before training and never changing them.
options.C: Increasing the learning rate only at inference time.
options.D: Replacing the loss function with accuracy.

rationales.correct: During training, dropout samples subnetworks by zeroing selected activations. The stochastic perturbation regularizes learning; inference uses the full network with appropriate scaling/implementation semantics.
rationales.B: The masks are stochastic during training, not permanent architecture deletions.
rationales.C: Dropout is not an inference-time learning-rate operation.
rationales.D: The training objective can remain cross-entropy or another chosen loss.

stem: A validation score looks excellent only after the same validation set has been used to tune dozens of hyperparameters. What is the main concern?

options.A: Selection overfitting: the validation set has become part of the tuning process and its score can become optimistic.
options.C: The validation set has become statistically independent of the tuning process.

rationales.correct: Repeatedly adapting decisions to validation results can overfit to that finite validation set. A final untouched test set or nested validation strategy is used when an unbiased final estimate matters.
rationales.B: Excellent tuned validation performance does not diagnose underfitting.
rationales.C: It is directly dependent because tuning decisions use it.
